title: Does drinking water hydrate your skin?

beats.vo: Drinking water for skin? Forty-nine women tested it.
beats.visual: Close-up of a single drop hitting the water in a glass (crown splash, ripples) for the first second; slide out to the glass on the counter in window light. '49 women' prints on the receipt on 'Forty-nine'. No hands.

beats.vo: The claim: drink more water, hydrate your skin. Let's check the receipt.
beats.visual: Receipt prints the claim in Courier Prime with printer ticks. Water pours into the glass from an out-of-frame stream. No hands.

beats.vo: Line one. Healthy women, aged twenty-two to thirty-four. They added about two liters a day, roughly eight glasses, for four weeks.
beats.visual: Receipt line 1 prints, then 'aged 22-34'. Eight glasses fill in a row from an out-of-frame pour stream, one per printer tick, sliding in and settling on their own. Lateral slide along the row. No hands.

beats.vo: Everyone got the extra water. Nobody was left as a comparison.
beats.visual: The row of glasses holds; a Slate dashed empty slot with a question mark prints at the end of the row. Slow push-in on the empty slot.

beats.vo: Food counted too. Over half their water came from food, soup and juice.
screen: over half of their water: food, soup, juice
beats.visual: A plate, a bowl of soup and a glass of juice slide in beside the row of glasses; a receipt tag prints 'over half'. Lateral slide across the table.

beats.vo: A probe then measured skin hydration. Forehead, forearm, hand, leg.
beats.visual: Macro of a small round probe touching a cheek of olive skin, then a forearm of dark brown skin. Lateral slide follows the probe.

beats.vo: In the thirty-eight who took in less water overall, the forehead reading rose about forty percent.
beats.visual: A Verified Teal bar prints on the strip rising from 54 to 76 on a simple scale. Locked-off; the bar grows on the word forty.

beats.vo: In the eleven who already drank a lot, the change wasn't clear.
beats.visual: A second bar, short and Slate, prints beside the first with a small 'not clear' tag. Static.

beats.vo: Skin's barrier, how fast water escapes, didn't really change.
screen: water loss through skin: no relevant change
beats.visual: Macro of a cheek of light skin, tiny water-droplet shapes sit on the surface and stay put. Slow hold.

beats.vo: Sounds like a win. But it's one small study.
beats.visual: The teal +40 % bar flashes back on 'Sounds like a win'; the 'one small study' tag lands over it.

beats.vo: A 2018 review of five studies like it called the evidence weak.
beats.visual: Five small receipts stack and print one by one, each stamped lightly; a Slate WEAK tag prints on top. Lateral slide down the stack.

beats.vo: And it's unclear whether you'd notice the difference in a mirror.
beats.visual: A real bathroom mirror on the tile wall reflects the forearm and the glass (no face). Slow push-in.
Receipt total line prints; a Slate UNKNOWN stamp lands in Courier Prime. Printer tick, hold 1 s stillness.

beats.vo: Water might nudge skin hydration readings, mostly if you drink little. Proven? Not yet.
screen: might nudge readings · mostly if you drink little
beats.visual: Calm pull-back from the stamp to the full receipt and the glass on the counter, soft light.

beats.vo: If your skin stays dry, a dermatologist can check yours.
beats.visual: Gentle lateral slide across a range of skin tones, final frame on the end-card text. Hold 1.8 s.

end_card.text: Receipt total: UNKNOWN · In one small study, skin hydration readings rose after extra water, mostly in people who took in less water. A 2018 review called the evidence weak. Education, not medical advice.

cover.headline: Does drinking water hydrate your skin?
